slides.text: A government agency just replaced Windows with a fully declarative Linux setup built from swappable pieces: OS, cloud, even the office suite. The goal: stop depending on one vendor's roadmap for basic computing. **Swapping the OS turned out to be the easy part.**

The operating system layer is NixOS: describe a machine in one config file, and it builds **the exact same system every time.** No drift between machines, no surprises from a vendor's patch. That's why platform teams reach for it when they don't trust someone else's roadmap.

France already ships a hardened NixOS build for its own agencies, and Germany runs a similar open desktop project. Three countries arrived at the same architecture on their own: **declarative infrastructure as the way out of vendor lock-in.**

Developers in the discussion weren't convinced the OS was the hard part. One argued the real blocker is the office suite: **LibreOffice and Collabora still can't match Microsoft 365's collaboration** without real friction for everyday teams.

Another pushed further: cloning Office feature-for-feature tops out well short of the original. One engineer put it at roughly **80% parity, at best,** and argued the real fix is rethinking the workflow, not building a lookalike of tools people already route around.

panel.small: one engineer's estimate for office clones

slides.text: A sharper pattern showed up in the same discussion for running this at scale: make every machine **read-only,** push configuration from one central source, and serve the package store over the network. That leaves nothing to patch by hand and nothing left to drift.

If you're chasing vendor lock-in at your own company, the infrastructure layer is usually the tractable part. **The tools people live in all day** are the hard part, and that's where most independence projects fail.

Has your team ever tried to replace a core vendor tool, the one people use every day, rather than the infrastructure behind it? What broke first?

**Save this** for the next time someone proposes "let's just self-host it."
